prize_parts.citation: For the discovery that multivalent biomolecules can demix by liquid-liquid phase separation, a physical-chemical principle for organizing the interior of cells

statement.case_for: I keep B044 as my single-part position. The scientific core is a physical-chemical principle: multivalent macromolecules demix into dense and dilute phases above a saturation concentration, and this explains how membraneless compartments form. It was shown in living embryos (Hyman and Brangwynne, 2009) and with purified components (Rosen, 2012), and the quantitative comparison of binary phase diagrams and measured saturation concentrations with polymer-physics theory has been reproduced in many laboratories over fifteen years. Nothing else on the shortlist gives chemistry a new general concept of molecular organisation in this way. I now propose a narrower citation: it credits the principle and the demonstration that it can operate with defined components, and makes no claim that every cellular condensate is a liquid or that function in vivo is settled.
statement.case_against: The round-1 exchange sharpened the objections rather than removing them. Linke, Aili and Chabes each doubt that in vivo relevance is established, and I have no new experiment to offer against that; my answer is only that the citation can rest on the principle. Pappu and Mittag, who supplied the sequence-grammar theory, are left out, and a three-name cut that separates Rosen from them is arguable. B044 has one explicit supporter (me) after round 1, so I cannot claim a committee centre of gravity. Colleagues may also still read the topic as cell biology.

responses.point: Linke argues that condensates are still debated in vivo and that a prize now would risk crediting a concept before its physiological scope is mapped, and he asks that the citation avoid claiming all condensates are liquid.
responses.response: I accept the drafting constraint fully: the revised citation speaks of multivalent biomolecules that can demix, not of all condensates being liquids. I do not accept that unresolved scope is disqualifying, because the same was true of other mechanisms that we honoured while their reach was being mapped. I also note that your own perovskite citation depends on the three-name cut among six claimants (Park versus Grätzel, Kanatzidis or Seok) being defensible, and I find the B044 attribution to the three experimentalists who established the principle no more contested than that. I rank B017 fifth because the efficiency record is in doubt in the early years and stability is open.

responses.point: Aili says B036 has a clear chemical identity and, unlike condensates, no comparable dispute about relevance, and he has ranked B044 sixth because of the in vivo debate and the omission of Pappu and Mittag.
responses.response: I agree that B036 has the stronger chemical identity and fewer open scientific questions, and that is why it stays my first alternative. The difference is attribution, not science. You concede that Hope, Madden and MacLachlan made decisive Vancouver contributions and that industry did much of the optimisation, and the files give me no way to decide whether Cullis, Hope and Madden (my opening cut) or Cullis, Anderson and Langer (yours) is the defensible trio. I would move to B036 if you and Linke could agree on a trio and a separable first step; the identical Cullis-led cut with Hope and Madden that Linke and I proposed in the opening ballots is not yours. On Pappu and Mittag, I accept the cost and note that the three-name limit forces it.

responses.point: Chabes is cautious about maturity: whether many condensates are phase separated at physiological concentrations in vivo is disputed, and a measured read-out of function is missing.
responses.response: That is a fair measurement point and I do not claim function is settled. The claim I am defending is narrower: that phase separation of defined multivalent components, with measured saturation concentrations, is a general mechanism, and that it is demonstrated in at least some living systems (P granules in the embryo). On your own B054 choice, I ranked it fourth and would accept Crews and Deshaies as the core, but I agree with you that a degrader prize without Handa and Ciulli, with no heterobifunctional drug approved, is the less mature configuration. I would not support a two-part Chabes prize that pairs B054 with B069, because the first is defined by a concept the second hardly shares.

responses.point: Brzezinski prefers B054 as a single-part prize for Crews, Deshaies and Handa, spanning heterobifunctional degraders and the cereblon glue mechanism.
responses.response: I find your unification of PROTACs and the cereblon glue mechanism as targeted degradation by induced proximity scientifically attractive, and it is a stronger case than splitting the field in two. My hesitation, shared with Chabes, is maturity, since no heterobifunctional degrader is approved. I put Ciulli in my own opening trio because structure-guided ligand design is physical chemistry. If the committee does select B054, I would favour your single-part framing over a pairing, but I would still want the committee to say why Ciulli rather than Handa.

uncertainties: Whether Linke, Aili and Chabes will accept a citation limited to the physical principle when they doubt the in vivo scope.
Whether a three-person cut of Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen can be defended against Pappu and Mittag.
Whether B036 attribution (Cullis, Hope and Madden versus Cullis, Anderson and Langer) can be resolved from the file, since I would then reconsider B036 as my preferred part.
Whether the committee prefers one coherent single-part prize to the two-part pairings proposed by Chabes and Somfai; I prefer a single part.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal need for any shortlisted candidate. My work on lipid self-assembly overlaps scientifically with B036, B044 and B069 but I have no personal tie to any candidate. I share Lund affiliation with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, which is not a conflict for any shortlisted candidate.
